doc.title: Tom Varner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 13, 2025

title: Free improvisation: Karl Berger, Braxton and the tightrope of freedom
summary: Reacting to quotes, he sets up structures, records short miniatures, and says free playing demands serious ideas; listeners and players may hear differently, e.g. Evan Parker.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I had a couple quotes here about free improv. And I wanted to share them with you, see if you have a reaction. The first one is from Karl Berger, who said to me, “More freedom is not about less precision, it’s about more precision. I’m creating my own rules and they’re much more stringent.” And Anthony Braxton, who I have not interviewed but I read this, he said, “I was never interested in runaway improvisation.”

I understand that quite well. I like to have, if it’s quote unquote free improvisation, whatever that means – I like to have the settings where it’s still I don’t want to say controlled like but I kind of am controlling it as a composer setting up a certain structure or guidelines for in the moment in which if I’m recording a series of improvisations they might be pretty short. So right there I might have, especially on the new things that I just did recently when I got a sabbatical and I was on the East Coast and I met with lots of

dear old friends and many new friends, and we would – we recorded many two-minute tracks. They were free but they were lots of little miniatures. And then the end product I would, with my decisions, put them together in interesting sequences basically. But when something is only two minutes you really just grab on to one or two ideas and let it be. If you want something to be totally free but 15, 18, 20 minutes, you better have, as Karl kind of was saying, and/or Braxton, some serious ideas up in your sleeve that you would be able to use. But you don’t want to just – but not as tricks. This is the thing. It’s a fine line. You don’t want to use them as little tricks but you don’t want to meander at the same time, like where do we go now, where do we go now. And so the mark of a really good improviser is like they’re able to make a statement with great intention. Make something with that. And then maybe at a certain point change. And when it’s two or three or four musicians and they change all at once it’s a wonderful moment when that happens I guess. So I like Karl’s quote in that in some ways it’s harder ‘cause you don’t have the safety of like okay as long as I play these chord changes within this time framework of “All the Things You Are” or whatever the tune it is, I won’t fail. It might not be great but it won’t be terrible. But if you’re playing very free and it’s a situation where you’re not relying on that it could be really good. But sometimes it could be pretty bad. It’s a little bit more of a tightrope one could say.
And what sounds acceptable to the person playing it may be different from with an audience person hears.

That is true. Sometimes the musician is like zeroing in maybe with another improviser together on some very specific strange little molecular grainy sound and you’re like, “Oh I like that” and you just want to stay there. Like zeroing in like the microscope. And certain listeners would be like, “Wow, oh that’s so great.” But other people are like, “Oh my God they’re playing the same weird little sound. But that’s just the nature of the beast. I don't know if you know the great British improviser Evan Parker. He will zero in on – well he’ll do duos, he used to do duos with Anthony Braxton and they might zero in on some one little sound and just stay there, or with circular breathing, or the overtones. Well you know as a saxophone, the overtones you could get and the harmonics and just stay in that one little place. So some people love it, some people like ahh.
